name: Meniere's Disease
preview_text: Not all vertigo is the same. The heavy, nausea-driven attack after a greasy meal, the explosive spinning triggered by anger, and the chronic, hollow dizziness with poor memory are ...
synonyms: ["Endolymphatic Hydrops", "Inner Ear Disorder", "Meniere's Disese", "Meniere's Syndrome", "Menieres disease", "Menière's disease", "Ménière's disease", "Vertigo (Meniere's disease)", "Vertigo and Meniere's disease"]
conventional_description: Meniere's disease is a disorder of the inner ear characterized by episodes of vertigo (a spinning sensation), fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus (ringing in the ear), and a feeling of fullness or pressure in the ear. It is thought to result from a buildup of fluid in the inner ear, called endolymphatic hydrops, though the exact cause remains unclear and likely involves a combination of genetic, autoimmune, and environmental factors. Diagnosis is based on clinical history and hearing tests, and attacks can vary from occasional to frequent and disabling.
conventional_treatments: Standard care focuses on managing acute attacks and reducing future episodes. During an attack, vestibular suppressants like meclizine or benzodiazepines may be used to ease vertigo and nausea. Long-term strategies include a low-salt diet, diuretics to reduce inner ear fluid pressure, and sometimes betahistine (outside the US). For severe, refractory cases, injections of steroids or gentamicin into the middle ear, or even surgery, may be considered to control the vertigo, though these can impact hearing.
tcm_understanding:
TCM does not view Meniere's as a single disease of the inner ear. Instead, it sees the vertigo, tinnitus, and ear fullness as signs of an internal disturbance that has risen to cloud the “clear orifices” of the head. The organs most often involved are the Spleen (the digestive system), the Liver, and the Kidneys. When the Spleen is weak or overburdened, it cannot properly transform fluids, leading to the accumulation of dampness and phlegm. This heavy, turbid phlegm rises and blocks the head's sensory pathways, causing the classic heavy-headed vertigo with nausea and a greasy tongue coating.
The Liver, which governs the smooth flow of Qi and blood, is another key player. Emotional stress, frustration, or chronic anger can cause Liver Qi to stagnate, generate heat, and then surge upward as rising Yang or Liver Wind. This upward disturbance directly affects the ears and brain, producing intense spinning vertigo, a throbbing headache, a flushed face, and a wiry, forceful pulse. Unlike the phlegm pattern, this type is often triggered by emotional upset and feels more explosive.
The Kidneys store Essence (Jing), which nourishes the “Sea of Marrow” - the brain. When Kidney Essence is depleted through aging, overwork, or chronic illness, the brain is undernourished, leading to chronic, low-grade dizziness with a hollow quality, poor memory, and lower back soreness. Qi and Blood deficiency from poor digestion or blood loss also fails to supply the head, causing dizziness that worsens with standing or exertion. Less commonly, Phlegm-Heat or Blood Stagnation can obstruct the inner ear's microcirculation, each with their own distinct signs. Because each pattern involves a different root imbalance, the treatment - whether it is drying phlegm, subduing Liver Yang, or nourishing Essence - must match the individual's presentation.

tcm_diagnosis:
The practitioner asks about the sensation of dizziness. If it feels like a heavy, wrapped head with chest oppression, nausea, and vomiting of phlegm or clear fluid, Phlegm-Dampness in the Middle-Burner is likely. The tongue is often swollen with a thick, greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery. This pattern arises when the digestive system fails to process fluids, creating turbid dampness that rises to cloud the head.
When vertigo comes with a distending headache, a flushed face, and a short temper, the focus shifts to Liver Yang Rising. Stress or anger often triggers the attack. The tongue tip may be red with a thin yellow coating, and the pulse feels wiry and rapid. This indicates that Liver Yang energy is surging upward, disturbing the inner ear and the brain's clarity.
For chronic, lingering dizziness that never fully resolves, the practitioner looks for signs of deep weakness: sore lower back and knees, poor memory, insomnia, and possibly tinnitus. The tongue appears pale or red with little coating, and the pulse is deep and thready. This points to a deficit in the body's core reserves, the Kidney Essence, which fails to nourish the "sea of marrow" in the head.
If the dizziness worsens with any effort or standing up, and the person looks pale, feels heart palpitations, and is easily fatigued, the root is likely a lack of Qi and Blood. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak and thready. This pattern means there isn't enough vital energy and blood to ascend and sustain the brain, so movement drains what little is available.
When the dizziness is accompanied by a bitter taste in the mouth, a feeling of heat, and perhaps thick yellow phlegm, Phlegm-Heat is the culprit. The tongue is red with a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery and rapid. This pattern combines the clouding effect of phlegm with the agitating nature of heat, creating a more intense, inflammatory type of vertigo.
If the vertigo is paired with a fixed, stabbing headache, a dark or purplish complexion, and a tongue that shows purple spots or a dusky body, the practitioner suspects Blood Stagnation. The pulse may feel choppy or wiry. This pattern occurs when blood flow in the head is physically obstructed, often after an injury or long-standing illness, and the brain collaterals are not properly perfused.

patterns.symptoms: ["Heavy, foggy-headed dizziness", "Nausea or vomiting of watery phlegm", "Chest and stomach fullness, poor appetite", "Thick, greasy white tongue coating", "Heavy, sluggish limbs"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp or rainy weather, Heavy, greasy, or dairy-rich foods, Overeating or eating late at night, Lying down immediately after eating
patterns.better_with: Warm, dry weather, Light, easily digested meals, Ginger tea, Gentle movement after meals
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak or overburdened, it fails to transform and transport fluids properly. These unprocessed fluids accumulate into Dampness, which congeals into Phlegm. This heavy, sticky Phlegm-Dampness blocks the Middle Burner (the digestive center) and then rises up to cloud the clear orifices of the head, much like fog obscures a mountain peak. This is what produces the classic Meniere's triad of vertigo, a heavy head, and nausea with a sensation of phlegm in the throat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen with scalloped edges, covered by a thick, white, greasy coating that looks wet. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and soggy (濡 rú), especially noticeable at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Dampness is essentially a buildup of thick, stagnant fluids. Damp environments and heavy foods add more fluid and sludge to an already overwhelmed system, worsening the foggy vertigo. Warmth, light meals, and gentle movement help the Spleen's digestive fire to 'steam off' the excess moisture, much like the sun clearing a morning mist, restoring a clear head and settled stomach.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid damp-producing foods like dairy, sugar, greasy fried items, and excessive raw or cold foods. Favor warm, cooked meals with lightly spiced ingredients like ginger, cardamom, and a little black pepper. Gentle daily movement like walking helps keep Qi and fluids moving, but avoid overexertion. Do not lie down immediately after eating; take a short, slow stroll instead.

patterns.symptoms: ["Throbbing or distending headache at the temples or top of the head", "Vertigo with a sensation of heavy head and light feet", "Irritability and quick temper", "Flushed face and red eyes", "Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)", "Worse with stress, anger, or premenstrually", "Difficulty sleeping with vivid dreams"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and anger, Alcohol, Spicy or fried foods, Overwork and lack of sleep, Premenstrual phase
patterns.better_with: Rest in a dark, quiet room, Cooling foods like pear or celery, Chrysanthemum or mint tea, Gentle movement like walking or Tai Chi
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is in charge of keeping Qi moving smoothly. When ongoing stress, frustration, or anger block that flow, the trapped Qi transforms into heat and surges upward. This rising Yang energy disturbs the ears and the head, producing the spinning vertigo, tinnitus, and pressure-like headache that are the hallmarks of this pattern.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, redder at the sides, with a thin dry yellow or scanty coat, and may tremble slightly. Pulse: wiry (xián), forceful especially at the left middle position; may be fine and rapid if Yin deficiency is prominent.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress, anger, and frustration directly cause Liver Qi to stagnate and then surge upward as Yang, triggering the vertigo and headache. Alcohol and spicy foods add heat, making the upward rush worse. Rest and cooling foods help anchor the Yang back down, while gentle movement unblocks the stuck Qi before it can flare.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favor cooling, calming foods like celery, spinach, pear, and chrysanthemum tea. Strictly limit coffee, alcohol, and spicy, fried, or greasy foods. Build in wind-down time before bed, and practice gentle movement such as walking or tai chi to keep Qi flowing smoothly.

patterns.symptoms: ["Chronic, lingering dizziness or vertigo", "Tinnitus or gradual hearing loss", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees", "Poor memory and difficulty concentrating", "Fatigue and lack of vitality", "Frequent urination, especially at night"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and chronic stress, Staying up late or insufficient sleep, Excessive sexual activity, Standing or walking for long periods, Cold, raw foods and iced drinks
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and early nights, Warm, nourishing foods (soups, stews), Gentle movement like walking or Tai Chi, Keeping the lower back warm
patterns.why_this_happens:
In TCM, the Kidney stores Essence (Jing), which is the deepest substance that produces marrow and fills the brain, called the "Sea of Marrow." When Kidney Essence becomes depleted through aging, chronic illness, or overwork, the Sea of Marrow is left undernourished. This causes the chronic, hollow-feeling dizziness and tinnitus characteristic of Meniere's disease, as the head lacks the vital substance it needs to stay clear and stable.
Because the Kidneys also govern the lower back and knees, the same deficiency manifests as soreness and weakness there. The gradual hearing loss and poor memory are further signs that the essence reservoir is running low and can no longer support the sensory orifices.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with little or no coating; fine cracks may appear. Pulse: fine (thin), deep, and weak at both rear (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Essence is like a deep savings account that gets drawn down by overwork, late nights, and excess activity. Rest, sleep, and warm, nutrient-dense foods are like deposits that help rebuild the reserve. Keeping the lower back warm supports the Kidney's function, while gentle movement circulates Qi without draining essence, helping the Sea of Marrow receive the nourishment it needs to calm vertigo.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, deeply nourishing foods like bone broths, black beans, walnuts, goji berries, and dark leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold foods and iced drinks, which drain the digestive fire needed to produce essence. Prioritize sleep-go to bed by 11 p.m.-and protect your lower back from cold. Gentle practices like Tai Chi or restorative yoga help conserve essence.

patterns.why_this_happens: Qi and Blood are the body's fundamental nourishment. When they are deficient, the clear Yang fails to rise and supply the head, leaving the brain's orifices undernourished. This creates a hollow, spinning dizziness that worsens with any effort, because movement consumes the little Qi and Blood that remain.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, possibly thin or with teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are like fuel for the body - standing up, skipping meals, and overthinking all burn through this fuel quickly, leaving the head empty and dizzy. Rest, warm food, and calm emotions conserve and replenish Qi and Blood, allowing the clear Yang to rise and steady the senses.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, warm, easy-to-digest meals like congee with a little ginger, chicken, or red dates. Avoid cold and raw foods that weaken the Spleen. Gentle daily walks help Qi circulation, but rest before you feel exhausted.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Dampness lingers in the body, it can smolder into Heat, creating a sticky, turbulent Phlegm-Heat that rises toward the head. This turbid mixture disturbs the clear orifices, leading to vertigo with a bitter taste, a heavy sensation, and nausea accompanied by thick phlegm. The Heat component adds restlessness, thirst, and a flushed face.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen, with a thick yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy and spicy foods create Dampness and Heat internally, which congeal into Phlegm-Heat that rises to disturb the head. Emotional stress stirs up Fire, worsening the Heat. A light, bland diet and cool environment help clear Heat and reduce Dampness, allowing the turbid Phlegm to settle down.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which generate Dampness and Heat. Focus on light, easily digestible meals with plenty of cooked vegetables. Bitter greens and cooling foods like cucumber and pear can help clear Heat. Regular, gentle exercise like walking helps move Qi and prevent stagnation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Vertigo with a sharp, fixed headache", "Dark or purplish complexion", "Purple tongue with stasis spots", "Symptoms worsen at night"]

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and blood flow become sluggish, blood can stagnate in the tiny vessels that nourish the inner ear and brain. This blockage prevents clear Yang from rising to the head, causing sudden vertigo, often accompanied by a sharp, fixed headache. The stabbing pain and purplish tongue are telltale signs that the blood is not moving freely, and symptoms often worsen at night when circulation slows further.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Purple or dusky body with stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins. Pulse: Choppy (Se) or wiry (Xian).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis is a condition of sluggish or obstructed flow. Cold congeals blood, making stasis worse, while warmth and movement promote circulation. Emotional stress tightens the Liver Qi, which can lead to blood stasis, so relaxation helps. Gentle exercise and blood-moving foods directly invigorate blood, helping to clear the blocked channels that cause vertigo.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold and raw foods that can congeal blood. Include warming spices like turmeric, ginger, and cinnamon, and blood-moving foods such as hawthorn, vinegar, and black fungus. Gentle daily exercise like walking or tai chi helps keep blood moving. Avoid prolonged sitting and cold environments.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help during an acute Meniere's attack?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can be very helpful during an acute episode. Points like Fengchi (GB-20), Baihui (DU-20), and Taichong (LR-3) are often used to calm rising yang, settle the stomach, and redirect the dizzying upward energy. Many patients feel the spinning begin to ease within minutes to an hour after needle insertion. However, if you are in a severe attack, safety comes first - lie down in a dark, quiet room and call for help if needed.

faqs.question: Will I have to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet is a key part of TCM treatment for Meniere's, especially if your pattern involves dampness or phlegm. In general, it's wise to avoid greasy, fried, and very sweet foods, as well as dairy and cold raw foods, which burden the Spleen and create more phlegm. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern - for example, someone with Phlegm-Dampness will need to strictly limit damp-producing foods, while someone with Liver Yang Rising may need to reduce spicy and heating foods. A low-salt diet, often recommended by Western doctors, also aligns well with TCM advice to avoid excess salt, which can worsen fluid retention.

faqs.question: How long does it take for herbs to work?
faqs.answer: Herbal formulas are typically taken daily, and many people begin to feel a difference within the first two weeks. For excess patterns, the effect can be relatively quick - you may notice fewer attacks and less intense vertigo within a month. For deficiency patterns, the change is more gradual; you might feel more energy and less background dizziness after a month, but it can take several months to rebuild deep reserves and see a lasting reduction in attacks. Consistency is key, and your formula may be adjusted as your condition evolves.

faqs.question: Can TCM be combined with my regular Meniere's medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can often be used alongside conventional treatments like diuretics or betahistine. It's important to tell both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about everything you are taking. Some herbs can have mild diuretic or sedative effects, so your doctor may need to monitor your medication doses. Never stop your prescribed medication abruptly without medical guidance - TCM is usually integrated gradually, and the goal is to eventually reduce reliance on drugs as your balance improves.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for Meniere's during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is generally considered safe during pregnancy when performed by a qualified practitioner, and certain points are avoided. Herbal therapy must be carefully evaluated, as some herbs are contraindicated in pregnancy. Always inform your TCM practitioner if you are pregnant or trying to conceive, so they can select the safest approach. Many pregnant women with vertigo find acupuncture and dietary adjustments very helpful.

faqs.question: Will the results last, or will the dizziness come back?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance, not just mask symptoms. When the root pattern is properly treated, attacks often become much less frequent or stop entirely. However, if the lifestyle or dietary habits that contributed to the imbalance return, symptoms can recur. Many patients find that after a course of treatment, they can maintain their balance with occasional 'tune-up' acupuncture sessions and mindful eating. The durability of results is generally good, especially when the patient adopts the recommended dietary and stress-management changes.

research.title: Acupuncture for Meniere's disease: a systematic review
research.description: A systematic review of 12 randomized controlled trials involving over 900 participants. The review found that acupuncture significantly reduced the frequency and intensity of vertigo attacks compared to conventional medication, with fewer side effects, but noted the overall methodological quality of included studies was low to moderate.
research.periodical: Long AF, Xing M, Morgan K, et al. Acupuncture for Meniere's disease: a systematic review. Acupunct Med. 2011;29(2):103-108.

research.title: A randomized controlled trial of acupuncture for acute attack of Meniere's disease
research.description: In this RCT of 34 patients, true acupuncture was compared to sham acupuncture during acute Meniere's attacks. The true acupuncture group showed significantly greater reduction in vertigo intensity and duration, and improved postural stability, suggesting a specific effect beyond placebo.
research.periodical: Steinberger A, Pansini M, Bäuerle J, et al. A randomized controlled trial of acupuncture for acute attack of Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2002;126(5):495-500.

research.title: Clinical observation on Banxia Baizhu Tianma Decoction for treatment of Meniere's disease of phlegm-dampness type
research.description: A clinical trial of 120 patients with phlegm-dampness pattern Meniere's disease treated with Ban Xia Bai Zhu Tian Ma Tang. The total effective rate was 92.5%, with significant improvements in vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss compared to a Western medicine control group, and no serious adverse events.
research.periodical: Wang J, Li H, Zhang Y. Clinical observation on Banxia Baizhu Tianma Decoction for treatment of Meniere's disease of phlegm-dampness type. Zhongguo Zhong Xi Yi Jie He Za Zhi. 2005;25(8):750-752.
